procedural_history.originating_court: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Rohini Courts, Delhi, in MAC Petition No. 4415 of 2016
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 11.05.2023 of the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi in MACAPP No.914 of 2019.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Delhi High Court reversed the Award dated 06.07.2018 passed by the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Rohini Courts, Delhi, in MAC Petition No. 4415 of 2016, to the extent it granted the right of recovery to the petitioner-insurance company. The High Court opined that the insurance company had neither pleaded nor proved that the deceased vehicle owner did not take adequate steps to verify the genuineness of the driving licence and in the absence of such a plea on its part, the Tribunal could not have concluded that there was a breach of the terms and conditions of the insurance policy.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: IFFCO Tokio General Insurance Co. Ltd. (the insurance company) filed a Special Leave Petition (C) No.19992 of 2023 in the Supreme Court to challenge the High Court's order. The Supreme Court dismissed the special leave petition.

issue.issue_text: Whether an insurance company has the right to recover compensation from the vehicle owner when the driver is found to have a fake driving license, in the absence of pleading and proof that the owner willfully breached the policy conditions by not verifying the license's genuineness.

facts: After a fatal motor vehicle accident, it was discovered that the driver of the vehicle had a fake driving license.
The deceased vehicle owner had hired the driver after seeing his license, which was not demonstrably fake on its face, and conducting a driving skill test.
The insurance company did not initially plead that the owner knew the license was fake or had willfully breached the policy. Their main defense was that the victim was negligent.
law: The burden of proof is on the insurance company to prove that the insured (vehicle owner) willfully breached a condition of the insurance policy.
The mere fact that a driver's license is later found to be fake is not, by itself, sufficient to absolve the insurer of liability.
To avoid liability, the insurer must prove that the owner was aware the license was fake or was negligent and failed to exercise reasonable care when hiring the driver.

Vehicle owners are generally not required by insurance policies to verify a driver's license with the transport authorities (RTO), as this is considered impracticable. An owner can be satisfied with a license that appears valid on its face.
application: The Supreme Court noted that the insurance company failed to plead and provide any proof that the vehicle owner knew the license was fake or had willfully neglected his duty.
The owner had taken reasonable steps by examining the license (which appeared valid) and testing the driver's skills.
Since the license was not obviously fake, the owner had no reason to be suspicious and undertake a formal verification with the RTO.

The court placed the responsibility squarely on the insurance company to prove a willful breach by the owner. As the company did not undertake this exercise, it could not claim that the policy conditions were violated.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the insurance company's claim to recover compensation from the vehicle owner. It held that in the absence of pleading and proof that the owner willfully breached the policy by knowingly hiring a driver with a fake license or by failing to exercise reasonable care, the insurer cannot recover the compensation amount. The burden was on the insurer to prove this willful breach, which it failed to do.

issue.issue_text: Whether the burden of proof is on the insurance company to establish that the vehicle owner committed a willful breach of the policy by failing to exercise due diligence in verifying the driver's license.

facts: After a motor vehicle accident, it was discovered that the driver of the vehicle had a fake driving license.
The vehicle owner had hired the driver after the driver produced a license that appeared to be valid.

The insurance company argued that the owner breached the policy conditions by not ensuring the driver was duly licensed, and therefore, the company had the right to recover the compensation paid from the owner.
law: The burden of proof is on the insurance company to establish that the insured (vehicle owner) committed a "willful breach" of the policy conditions.
A 'breach' implies a willful infringement or violation. The insurer must prove that the insured was at fault and failed to exercise reasonable care.
Merely proving that the driver's license was fake is not, by itself, sufficient for the insurer to avoid liability.

When an owner is presented with a "seemingly valid" driving license, they are generally not required to verify its genuineness with the transport authorities, unless the license is demonstrably fake on its face, expired, or there is another clear reason to doubt its validity.
application: The Court noted that the insurance company had not even pleaded (formally argued) that the vehicle owner knowingly hired a driver with a fake license.
The insurance policy itself did not contain a condition requiring the owner to get the driver's license verified by the RTO (Regional Transport Office).
The Court found it would be impractical to expect every person employing a driver to undertake such a verification exercise.

Since the driver had produced a seemingly valid license and there was no evidence to suggest the owner should have been suspicious, the burden was on the insurance company to prove that the owner failed to exercise due diligence.
The insurance company failed to present any evidence to show that the owner had willfully breached the policy.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the burden of proof is on the insurance company to prove that the vehicle owner committed a willful breach of the policy by failing to exercise due diligence. Because the insurance company failed to provide any such proof, it was held liable and could not recover the compensation amount from the vehicle's owners.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an insurance company has the right to recover compensation from the vehicle owner when the driver is found to have a fake driving license, in the absence of pleading and proof that the owner willfully breached the policy conditions by not verifying the license's genuineness.
appellant_arguments: The fact that the driver's license was fake constitutes a breach of the insurance policy, which grants the company the right to recover compensation from the vehicle owner.
The evidence provided by the vehicle owner's widow about a driving skill test being conducted was mere hearsay without corroboration and should be dismissed.
respondent_arguments: The insurance company must plead and prove a *willful* breach by the owner, not just the existence of a fake license.
The insurance policy did not require the vehicle owner to verify the driver's license with the RTO.
The owner acted with due diligence by checking a seemingly valid license and was not aware it was fake.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the burden of proof is on the insurance company to establish that the vehicle owner committed a willful breach of the policy by failing to exercise due diligence in verifying the driver's license.
appellant_arguments: The discovery of a fake license is sufficient proof of a policy breach, which should shift the burden to the vehicle owner to prove they exercised due diligence.
respondent_arguments: The burden of proof lies with the insurance company to establish that the vehicle owner willfully breached the policy conditions.

Unless a license is demonstrably fake or there is a clear reason for suspicion, the owner is not obligated to conduct an investigation into its genuineness; the insurer must prove the owner failed in their duty.

cases.case_name: Skandia Insurance Co. Ltd. vs. Kokilaben Chandravadan and others
cases.principle: Cited for its interpretation of a provision (Section 96(2)(b)(ii) of the 1939 Act) that is in pari materia with Section 149(2)(a)(ii) of the 1988 Act, establishing the insurer's burden to prove a breach of policy conditions to avoid liability.

cases.case_name: National Insurance Co. Ltd. vs. Swaran Singh and others
cases.principle: For an insurer to avoid liability towards an insured due to a breach of the policy condition regarding the driver's license, the breach must be fundamental and found to have contributed to the cause of the accident. The burden is on the insurer to prove such a breach, and how this burden is discharged depends on the facts of each case.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: To avoid liability for a policy breach, such as the driver having a fake license, an insurance company bears the burden of pleading and proving that the insured vehicle owner committed a willful breach. When an owner is presented with a seemingly valid driving license, the insurer must prove the owner failed in their due diligence, which is only required if the license was demonstrably fake, expired, or there was another specific reason to doubt its validity.
obiter: It is shocking that insurance companies raise pleas regarding policy breaches as a matter of course, without reference to the specific facts or evidence, and pursue such matters in appeal to the highest court, thereby wasting valuable judicial time.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: An insurance company cannot recover compensation from the vehicle owner merely because the driver's license was found to be fake. The insurer bears the burden of pleading and proving that the owner committed a willful breach of the policy conditions. This requires showing that the owner failed to exercise due diligence, such as when a license is demonstrably fake on its face or there is another clear reason to be suspicious, which would obligate the owner to verify its genuineness. In the absence of such proof, the insurer remains liable.
legal_tests_applied: The burden of proof is on the party alleging a breach of contract; therefore, the insurance company must establish that the insured willfully violated a policy condition.
To avoid liability, an insurer must prove not only a breach of a policy condition (like the driver not being duly licensed) but also that the breach was willful on the part of the insured.

An owner is considered to have exercised due diligence when presented with a seemingly valid driving license, unless the license is demonstrably fake on its face, has expired, or there is some other specific reason to entertain a genuine doubt as to its validity.

The 'rule of main purpose' and the concept of 'fundamental breach' apply, meaning an insurer may not be able to avoid liability unless the breach of the policy condition is so fundamental that it contributed to the cause of the accident.
why_appellant_lost: The insurance company failed to plead and prove that the vehicle owner committed a *willful* breach of the policy condition; merely establishing that the license was fake is insufficient.

The appellant did not meet its burden of proof to show that the insured failed to exercise due diligence. No evidence was presented to suggest the owner should have been suspicious of the license and was therefore obligated to verify it.
The argument that the owner should have conducted a driving skill test was rejected, as there was no such mandate in the statute or the specific insurance policy.
The insurance company failed to establish that the insured 'used or caused or permitted to be used the insured vehicle in breach of the provisions,' which is a necessary element to avoid liability.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully established that the burden of proof lies with the insurance company to prove a willful breach by the insured, and the insurer failed to discharge this burden.

The law does not obligate a vehicle owner to investigate the genuineness of a driver's license with the issuing authority unless there is a clear reason for suspicion, which the insurer did not prove existed in this case.
The court affirmed the principle that for an insurer to avoid liability, it must prove the insured was 'guilty of an infringement or violation of a promise' and that such violation was 'wilful'.
policy_considerations: The court expressed strong disapproval of insurance companies raising such pleas 'as a matter of course' and pursuing them to the highest court, viewing it as a 'wastage of valuable curial time and eﬀort'.

Statutory provisions allowing insurers to defend against claims should not be interpreted in an overly technical manner; the focus should be on whether the insured knowingly allowed the vehicle to be driven by an unlicensed person.

The expression 'breach' in the context of insurance policies implies a willful infringement or violation of a promise by the insured, not merely the existence of a condition that technically violates the policy but was unknown to the insured.
